ch23:label: Chapter 23
ch23:title: Salvation
ch23:0: Through Part 5 this book has examined who God is, what kind of being man is, and what the life of Jesus revealed. Part 6 asks where all those doctrines touch human life: how does man reach God? The first question is salvation. What is salvation, and by what is it received? And why does The Urantia Book call salvation a gift rather than a price paid or a reward earned? This chapter works through these questions starting from a more fundamental doctrine, the fatherhood of God.
ch23:1: 1. Definition: Salvation Is the Gift of God
ch23:2: Jesus gathered his teaching on salvation into a single statement. Salvation is not something a person buys or earns. It is something given.

ch23:3.q: You cannot buy salvation; you cannot earn righteousness. Salvation is the gift of God, and righteousness is the natural fruit of the spirit-born life of sonship in the kingdom.

ch23:4: The order in this statement matters. Salvation comes first, and righteousness follows afterward as its fruit. What, then, is the hand that receives the gift? Earlier in the same discourse Jesus calls that hand faith.

ch23:5.q: Salvation is the gift of the Father and is revealed by his Sons. Acceptance by faith on your part makes you a partaker of the divine nature, a son or a daughter of God. By faith you are justified; by faith are you saved; and by this same faith are you eternally advanced in the way of progressive and divine perfection.

ch23:6: This passage shows the three elements of salvation at once. The gift comes from the Father, the Sons reveal it, and man receives it by faith. In the moment of receiving, a person becomes a son or a daughter of God, and that sonship opens onto an endless path toward perfection. Salvation is not a passive event of escaping punishment but an active event of entering the family of God. Yet even that faith is not a merit that man produces by himself: “Even this saving faith you have not of yourselves; it also is the gift of God”(143:2.7). Both the gift and the hand that receives it come from above. What man does is open that hand, that is, choose to receive.
ch23:7: 2. Foundation: The Father Asks No Price
ch23:8: Why is salvation a gift? The answer lies not within the doctrine of salvation but within the doctrine of God. The shape of salvation is determined by what kind of being God is. Paper 2 first makes clear toward what the whole of creation is directed.

ch23:9.q: And the whole scheme of living existences on the worlds of space is centered in the divine purpose of elevating all will creatures to the high destiny of the experience of sharing the Father's Paradise perfection. God is neither self-centered nor self-contained

ch23:10: Salvation is not an emergency measure added after creation. The plan to elevate all will creatures to Paradise has been the central purpose of the universe from the beginning. If God is one who never ceases to bestow himself, then salvation is simply one way in which that bestowal reaches man. And the one who bestows it is not divided between justice and mercy.

ch23:11.q: The affectionate heavenly Father, whose spirit indwells his children on earth, is not a divided personality—one of justice and one of mercy—neither does it require a mediator to secure the Father's favor or forgiveness. Divine righteousness is not dominated by strict retributive justice; God as a father transcends God as a judge.

ch23:12: If God were only a judge, salvation would be a matter of paying a penalty and settling a debt. But if God is a Father, salvation becomes the child's recognition of the Father's love and return to his embrace. When Peter and James disputed over the order of forgiveness, Jesus explained this difference with an analogy from family life.

ch23:13.q: Divine forgiveness is inevitable; it is inherent and inalienable in God's infinite understanding, in his perfect knowledge of all that concerns the mistaken judgment and erroneous choosing of the child. Divine justice is so eternally fair that it unfailingly embodies understanding mercy.

ch23:14: If forgiveness is inherent in God, where does the sense of separation come from? Jesus says it lies on man's side, not on God's: “Sin is an experience of creature consciousness; it is not a part of God's consciousness”(174:1.4). Salvation, therefore, is not a matter of changing God's mind but of changing man's consciousness.

ch23:15.cap: Table 23.1  Two Concepts of God and the Views of Salvation That Follow
rows: God seen only as a judge
Divided between justice and mercy (denied by 2:6.6)
A mediator and a price are required
Something obtained by paying a price

ch23:16: 3. What Salvation Is Not: Atonement and Ransom
ch23:17: This line of reasoning immediately collides with an old view of salvation: the idea that an angry God must be appeased by the shedding of blood. In Paper 4 The Urantia Book says this idea arose from primitive religion and declares flatly: “It is an affront to God to believe, hold, or teach that innocent blood must be shed in order to win his favor or to divert the fictitious divine wrath”(4:5.4). Then, in section 4 of Paper 188, which treats the meaning of the cross, it applies this directly to the death of Jesus.

ch23:18.q: Jesus did not die this death on the cross to atone for the racial guilt of mortal man nor to provide some sort of effective approach to an otherwise offended and unforgiving God

ch23:19: This denial means that salvation is not bound to the death of Jesus. The way of salvation existed before it, and the bestowal of Jesus did not create that way anew but brightly illuminated it.

ch23:20.q: While the mortals of the realms had salvation even before Jesus lived and died on Urantia, it is nevertheless a fact that his bestowal on this world greatly illuminated the way of salvation; his death did much to make forever plain the certainty of mortal survival after death in the flesh.

ch23:21: This does not make the cross meaningless. The same section says that “it is wholly correct to refer to him as a savior”(188:4.7). He did not manufacture salvation; he illuminated its way. And the text sums up what salvation rests upon in these words.

ch23:22.q: Human salvation is real; it is based on two realities which may be grasped by the creature's faith and thereby become incorporated into individual human experience: the fact of the fatherhood of God and its correlated truth, the brotherhood of man.

ch23:23: The idea of atonement relocates salvation to a transaction in a heavenly court. But the text says that this concept “places salvation upon a plane of unreality”(188:4.13). True salvation stands upon two realities grasped within human experience: the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. And so the doctrine of salvation leads directly to the doctrine of the kingdom of heaven, which Chapter 25 takes up.

ch23:24.cap: Table 23.2  Ideas About the Cross and the Answer of the Text
rows: A death to atone for mankind's guilt
He did not die for that purpose
A ransom paid to fallen rulers
A sacrifice to pay a debt owed to God
It was not a sacrifice to pay a debt
There was no salvation before Jesus
Mortals had salvation even before him
What truly matters about the cross
Not the fact of his death but the manner and spirit in which he met it

ch23:26: If salvation is not the paying of a debt, what is its real content? The Urantia Book defines salvation as a change that takes place within a person. The definition comes from a conversation Jesus had in Rome during his younger years.

ch23:27.q: Salvation is the spiritualization of the self-realization of the moral consciousness, which thereby becomes possessed of survival value.

ch23:28: When the moral consciousness is spiritualized, the soul gains survival value. The end of salvation is survival, and its beginning is being born of the spirit. Jesus told Nicodemus that a person must be born again from above, and when asked how that birth comes about, he pointed to the spirit already within man. When Nicodemus asked how he could begin to lay hold upon that spirit, Jesus answered.

ch23:29.q: Already does the spirit of the Father in heaven indwell you. If you would be led by this spirit from above, very soon would you begin to see with the eyes of the spirit, and then by the wholehearted choice of spirit guidance would you be born of the spirit since your only purpose in living would be to do the will of your Father who is in heaven.

ch23:30: Being born again is not a matter of bringing something in from outside. It is choosing to accept the leading of the Father's spirit, the Thought Adjuster, who already indwells. The Adjuster was treated in Chapter 11. What matters here is that the initiative in salvation once again lies with God. The spirit has already come, and man wholeheartedly chooses its guidance. Hence Jesus summed up the way of salvation like this.

ch23:31.q: Salvation is by the regeneration of the spirit and not by the self-righteous deeds of the flesh. You are justified by faith and fellowshipped by grace, not by fear and the self-denial of the flesh

ch23:32: Salvation is not an event finished once and for all but an expanding experience. Paper 101 unfolds the salvation to which the faith of Jesus pointed in seven phases. Beginning with deliverance from material fetters and reaching to salvation from finity itself, this sevenfold salvation is a single path that begins now and continues into eternity. The first three phases can already be tasted in this earthly life, the fourth and fifth are completed in the ascending career, and the sixth and seventh in eternity. The same paper says that all of this is potentially contained in the religious experience of man (101:6.16). Salvation is not a reward first received after death, but the endless unfolding of a gift accepted now.

ch23:33.cap: Table 23.3  The Sevenfold Salvation to Which the Faith of Jesus Pointed (101:6.9–15)
rows: Realizing sonship with God, who is spirit (101:6.9)
Realizing brotherhood and discovering spiritual reality through service (101:6.11)
Attaining the harmony of Havona and the perfection of Paradise (101:6.12)
Attaining the cosmic levels of the Supreme Mind (101:6.13)
An eternal life of unending progression (101:6.14)
Perfected oneness with Deity in and through the Supreme (101:6.15)

ch23:34: 5. Sin and Forgiveness: What Blocks Salvation
ch23:35: If it is possible to refuse the gift, what leads someone to refuse it? The Urantia Book redefines sin not as a list of deeds but as a state of relationship.

ch23:36.q: Sin must be redefined as deliberate disloyalty to Deity. There are degrees of disloyalty: the partial loyalty of indecision; the divided loyalty of confliction; the dying loyalty of indifference; and the death of loyalty exhibited in devotion to godless ideals.

ch23:37: Two things follow from this definition. First, sin is not inherited. Animal tendencies may be passed on, but “sin is not transmitted from parent to child”(188:4.5). Second, the sense of guilt is not the same as sin. Awareness of having broken a moral code is not in itself sin; where there is no conscious disloyalty to Deity, there is no real sin (89:10.3). Indeed, the very capacity to feel guilt points to man's nobility.

ch23:38.q: The possibility of the recognition of the sense of guilt is a badge of transcendent distinction for mankind. It does not mark man as mean but rather sets him apart as a creature of potential greatness and ever-ascending glory.

ch23:39: The sense of guilt is given not to drive a person into despair but as the first stimulus toward faith. What blocks salvation, therefore, is not human weakness but the refusal of the will. Paper 2 does not hide the outcome when that refusal persists to the end: “The final result of wholehearted sin is annihilation”(2:3.2). God does not force survival on one who finally refuses it. This question of choice returns in Chapter 26.

rows: Belongs to the animal nature and may be hereditary
Awareness of violating the mores, not necessarily sin
A manful repudiation of disloyalty, essential to spiritual progress

ch23:41: 6. Consequence: The Life of the Saved
ch23:42: If salvation is a gift, what place do good works hold? Jesus reversed the order of works and salvation. Works are not the means of earning salvation but the fruit borne by one who has been saved.

ch23:43.q: You are not to be saved because you live a righteous life; rather is it that you live a righteous life because you have already been saved, have recognized sonship as the gift of God and service in the kingdom as the supreme delight of life on earth.

ch23:44: This order turns the believer's attention from self to neighbor. One who strives to earn salvation is always anxious about his own salvation, but one who has received it is freed from that anxiety and can serve others. Paper 188 makes the point clearly.

ch23:45.q: Salvation should be taken for granted by those who believe in the fatherhood of God. The believer's chief concern should not be the selfish desire for personal salvation but rather the unselfish urge to love and, therefore, serve one's fellows even as Jesus loved and served mortal men.

ch23:46: Jesus drew this whole movement in a single line: “The goodness of God leads to repentance; the beneficence of God leads to service; the mercy of God leads to salvation; while the love of God leads to intelligent and freehearted worship”(149:6.4). The starting point always lies with God, and man's repentance, service, and worship are the response. Even repentance is not wrung out of fear; it arises of itself when one sees the goodness of God. Jesus meant the same thing when he said that “Realization of sonship is incompatible with the desire to sin”(150:5.5). The power that separates a person from sin is not the threat of punishment but the awareness of being a child of God.

ch23:47.cap: Table 23.5  The Logical Chain of Salvation
rows: Salvation is the gift of God, received by faith
God is a Father before he is a judge
It begins with the regeneration of the spirit and reaches survival value
Sin, that is, deliberate disloyalty to Deity
A righteous life and service to one's fellows grow as its fruit

ch23:48: In Closing: Salvation Begins with the Father
ch23:49: The doctrine of salvation in The Urantia Book stands upon a single fact: God is a Father. Forgiveness therefore already exists in God, salvation is received as a gift rather than bought with a price, and even the faith that receives the gift is grace. The ideas of atonement and ransom cannot be reconciled with this concept of God as Father. The real content of salvation is to be born again of the spirit, so that the moral consciousness is spiritualized and the soul gains survival value, and its fruit is service to one's neighbor. At every joint in this chain stands faith. The next chapter examines what that faith is, how it differs from mere belief, and how it becomes the way of knowing God.

ch23:50.title: Questions for Reflection
items: 1. What change does the statement “God as a father transcends God as a judge”(2:6.6) ask of the fear or calculation I bring when I approach God?
2. If a righteous life is not the condition of salvation but its fruit (150:5.5), where do I find my motive for doing good?
3. If sin is seen as “deliberate disloyalty to Deity”(89:10.2), where in my life do the partial loyalty of indecision or the divided loyalty of confliction appear?

ch24:label: Chapter 24
ch24:title: Faith
ch24:0: The previous chapter ended with the point that salvation is a gift received by faith. What, then, is faith? Is it the mind's acceptance of a doctrine as correct? Is it an attitude of being sure of something without evidence? The Urantia Book rejects both answers. Faith is the way by which man knows God, a function of the soul that reaches spiritual reality at the point where reason and wisdom come to a halt. This chapter examines in turn the definition of faith and its source, its relation to reason, its fruits, and its great example, the faith of Jesus.
ch24:1: 1. Definition: Belief and Faith Are Different
ch24:2: Before it speaks of faith, The Urantia Book first distinguishes belief from faith. The title of section 8 of Paper 101 is precisely “Faith and Belief.” Its opening sentence draws the boundary between the two in the mode of living.

ch24:3.q: Belief has attained the level of faith when it motivates life and shapes the mode of living. The acceptance of a teaching as true is not faith; that is mere belief. Neither is certainty nor conviction faith. A state of mind attains to faith levels only when it actually dominates the mode of living.

ch24:4: What distinguishes faith, therefore, is not so much what one believes as whether that belief moves one's life. Of two people who confess the same doctrine, one may remain at belief while the other reaches faith. The passage that follows contrasts the character of the two.

ch24:5.q: Belief is always limiting and binding; faith is expanding and releasing. Belief fixates, faith liberates. But living religious faith is more than the association of noble beliefs; it is more than an exalted system of philosophy; it is a living experience concerned with spiritual meanings, divine ideals, and supreme values; it is God-knowing and man-serving

ch24:6: “It is God-knowing and man-serving.” This one phrase holds both directions of faith. Upward, it knows God; outward, it serves man. Faith is not a state that stays inside one's thoughts but a form of life. Moreover, beliefs may be held by a group in common, but faith grows only in the heart of the individual (101:8.2). A creed can be handed down; faith cannot. The faith of parents can show their children the way, but the children gain faith only by walking that way on their own feet.
ch24:7: There is also a misunderstanding that equates faith with emotional exaltation. But if faith is the way of knowing God, it must go beyond feeling and arrive at knowing. Paper 103 makes this clear.

ch24:8.q: Faith leads to knowing God, not merely to a mystical feeling of the divine presence. Faith must not be overmuch influenced by its emotional consequences. True religion is an experience of believing and knowing as well as a satisfaction of feeling.

ch24:9: Feelings rise and fall, but knowing remains. The depth of faith is not measured by how moved one is in prayer but by a life that goes on trusting God even on the days when that feeling has gone. Seen this way, the distinctions between belief and faith, and between feeling and faith, finally come down to one question: does that state of mind govern the life?

ch24:10.cap: Table 24.1  The Difference Between Belief and Faith
rows: A state of mind that actually dominates the mode of living (101:8.1)
Rises up only in the heart of the individual religionist (101:8.2)
May not be able to resist doubt and withstand fear (102:6.7)

ch24:12: If faith is not certainty without evidence, on what does its assurance rest? The Urantia Book explains faith as the working of a spiritual endowment given within man.

ch24:13.q: Faith-insight, or spiritual intuition, is the endowment of the cosmic mind in association with the Thought Adjuster, which is the Father's gift to man.

ch24:14: Faith is not a psychological state that a person squeezes out alone. It is a spiritual intuition that arises when the human mind works together with the indwelling Adjuster. Alongside it the same passage names spiritual reason, given by the Holy Spirit, and spiritual philosophy, given by the Spirit of Truth. When these three endowments are co-ordinated, man becomes “a spirit personality in potential destiny”(101:3.2). This is also why Paper 1 says that the existence of God is “utterly beyond all possibility of demonstration”(1:2.8) except for the contact between the God-consciousness of the human mind and the God-presence of the Adjuster. What faith lays hold of is not a fact proved from outside but a presence experienced within.

ch24:15.cap: Table 24.2  The Three Spirit Endowments in Man (101:3.2)
rows: The cosmic mind in association with the Adjuster, who is the Father's gift
The Holy Spirit, the gift of the Creative Spirit
The Spirit of Truth, the gift of the bestowal Sons

ch24:16: This table shows once more why faith is a gift. The spiritual intuition underlying faith comes from the Father's Adjuster; the spiritual reason that understands it comes from the Creative Spirit; and the spiritual philosophy that weaves it into the wisdom of life comes from the Spirit of Truth of the bestowal Sons. The statement in the previous chapter that even saving faith is the gift of God (143:2.7) here gains its structure. Faith is something man does, but not something man does alone.
ch24:18: If faith goes beyond proof, does it stand against reason? The Urantia Book places the two as acts of recognition in different domains.

ch24:19.q: Reason is the act of recognizing the conclusions of consciousness with regard to the experience in and with the physical world of energy and matter. Faith is the act of recognizing the validity of spiritual consciousness—something which is incapable of other mortal proof.

ch24:20: Reason and faith do not quarrel over the same object. Reason recognizes consciousness concerning the material world; faith recognizes spiritual consciousness. Faith therefore does not set out by abandoning reason. On the contrary, it travels with reason as far as reason can go.

ch24:21.q: Faith most willingly carries reason along as far as reason can go and then goes on with wisdom to the full philosophic limit; and then it dares to launch out upon the limitless and never-ending universe journey in the sole company of TRUTH.

ch24:22: On this journey there is one gap that reason alone cannot cross. Man can experience God as truth, yet he knows little of the fact of God. Paper 102 describes that gap this way.

ch24:23.q: The vast gulf between the experience of the truth of God and ignorance as to the fact of God can be bridged only by living faith. Reason alone cannot achieve harmony between infinite truth and universal fact.

ch24:24: Is faith, then, an assumption made without grounds? Paper 103 says that science and philosophy also each stand upon assumptions that cannot be proved. Faith is not uniquely weak in its grounds.

ch24:25.q: Science (knowledge) is founded on the inherent (adjutant spirit) assumption that reason is valid, that the universe can be comprehended. Philosophy (co-ordinate comprehension) is founded on the inherent (spirit of wisdom) assumption that wisdom is valid, that the material universe can be co-ordinated with the spiritual. Religion (the truth of personal spiritual experience) is founded on the inherent (Thought Adjuster) assumption that faith is valid, that God can be known and attained.

ch24:26.cap: Table 24.3  Science, Philosophy, Religion, and the Three Inherent Assumptions (103:9.8–10)
rows: Assumption on which it is founded
Reason is valid; the universe can be comprehended (adjutant spirit)
Wisdom is valid; the material universe can be co-ordinated with the spiritual (spirit of wisdom)
Faith is valid; God can be known and attained (Thought Adjuster)

ch24:27: The three assumptions do not cancel one another. The realization of the reality of mortal life consists in a progressive belief in the assumptions of reason, wisdom, and faith (103:9.9). Faith is not the enemy of reason but a companion that carries the road onward where reason ends. Just as a scientist begins research by assuming that the universe can be understood, a believer begins a life of prayer and obedience by assuming that God can be known. And that assumption is confirmed in experience. It is also worth noting that the three assumptions are rooted respectively in the adjutant spirit, the spirit of wisdom, and the Thought Adjuster. Even the ground on which man trusts that anything can be known is an endowment given from above.
ch24:29: If faith is an act of recognizing spiritual reality, how does one know that it is true? The Urantia Book locates the evidence in the fruits that faith bears in life. Section 3 of Paper 101 lists twelve ways in which genuine spiritual faith shows itself. They share one feature: the more circumstances run against faith, the more clearly faith appears.

ch24:30.cap: Table 24.4  Twelve Marks of Genuine Spiritual Faith (101:3.5–16)
rows: A sublime trust in the goodness of God (101:3.6)
Faith in the survival of the soul (101:3.12)
The overwhelming burden of modern civilization
The presence of evil and sin
Belief in universe unity and divine guidance (101:3.15)

ch24:31: Faith is not a burden but a power. Lamenting that people go hungry in the very presence of the bread of life, Jesus described the place of faith like this.

ch24:32.q: Faith is to religion what sails are to a ship; it is an addition of power, not an added burden of life. There is but one struggle for those who enter the kingdom, and that is to fight the good fight of faith. The believer has only one battle, and that is against doubt—unbelief.

ch24:33: A sail does not make the wind that moves the ship. It only catches it. Faith likewise does not produce spiritual power but receives it. That is why faith does not make a person heavier but carries him farther. Paper 101 emphasizes the path that this faith opens to man by repeating the word ‘only.’

ch24:34.q: Such faith affords the only escape from the mechanical clutch of the material world and from the error distortion of the incompleteness of the intellectual world; it is the only discovered solution to the impasse in mortal thinking regarding the continuing survival of the individual personality. It is the only passport to completion of reality and to eternity of life in a universal creation of love, law, unity, and progressive Deity attainment.

ch24:35: The statement that faith is the passport to eternity of life links the doctrine of salvation in the previous chapter with the eternal life of Chapter 26. Faith is the hand that receives salvation and also the door to the road toward survival. Its result appears as social fruit. Paper 102 says that the convincing evidence of spiritual certainty “consists in the social fruits of the spirit”(102:6.7) which such believers yield.
ch24:36: 5. The Example: The Faith of Jesus
ch24:37: The Urantia Book finds the highest example of faith in Jesus. Paper 196, “The Faith of Jesus,” says that his faith was neither intellectual reflection nor mystical meditation but a living faith (196:0.4), and it describes its quality like this.

ch24:38.q: The faith of Jesus attained the purity of a child's trust. His faith was so absolute and undoubting that it responded to the charm of the contact of fellow beings and to the wonders of the universe. His sense of dependence on the divine was so complete and so confident that it yielded the joy and the assurance of absolute personal security.

ch24:39: Yet this faith was not blind. The same paper says that the faith of Jesus was never fanatical and never sought to run away with his balanced intellectual judgments (196:0.7). Childlike trust and mature judgment dwelt together in one personality. That trust was not weakness; it was paired with a strong will.

ch24:40.q: The faith of Jesus was trusting, like that of a child, but it was wholly free from presumption. He made robust and manly decisions, courageously faced manifold disappointments, resolutely surmounted extraordinary difficulties, and unflinchingly confronted the stern requirements of duty.

ch24:41: Trust and resolution look like different virtues, but in Jesus they were one. Because he trusted the Father completely, he did not retreat even before disappointment. And what Jesus asked of people was to share this faith. Paper 196 says that “Jesus does not require his disciples to believe in him but rather to believe with him”(196:0.13). What sharing that faith opens up is made clear in Paper 101.

ch24:42.q: Through the appropriation of the faith of Jesus, mortal man can foretaste in time the realities of eternity. Jesus made the discovery, in human experience, of the Final Father, and his brothers in the flesh of mortal life can follow him along this same experience of Father discovery.

ch24:43: This shift, from believing in Jesus to believing with Jesus, is the center of this chapter. To follow Jesus goes beyond accepting doctrines about him; it is to trust the Father in the very way he trusted the Father. If Jesus discovered the Father in human experience, his brothers can follow the same experience. On the faith of Jesus and the faith of his disciples, see also Chapters 19 and 27.
ch24:44: 6. The Growth of Faith and Doubt
ch24:45: If faith is a struggle against doubt, does the one who doubts have no faith? The Urantia Book does not regard honest doubt as sin. It does, however, distinguish the beginning of faith from its progress.

ch24:46.q: But honest doubts and sincere questionings are not sin; such attitudes merely spell delay in the progressive journey toward perfection attainment. Childlike trust secures man's entrance into the kingdom of heavenly ascent, but progress is wholly dependent on the vigorous exercise of the robust and confident faith of the full-grown man.

ch24:47: To enter through the door, a child's trust is enough. But to walk the road, the faith of an adult is needed. That faith does not stop thought. On the contrary, “truth can never become man's possession without the exercise of faith”(132:3.5). At the same time, The Urantia Book warns against the cases in which faith betrays itself.

ch24:48.cap: Table 24.5  When Faith Betrays Itself, and Living Faith (101:8.3–4)
rows: When it seeks to deny reality and confer assumed knowledge (101:8.3)
Does not shirk the duty of problem solving (101:8.3)
Does not foster bigotry, persecution, or intolerance (101:8.3)
When it belittles loyalty to supreme values and divine ideals (101:8.3)
Does not shackle the creative imagination (101:8.4)
When it maintains unreasoning prejudice toward scientific discoveries (denied by 101:8.4)
Leads the religionist to live the golden rule heroically (101:8.4)

ch24:49: The growth of faith can be measured not by the size of one's certainty but by one's openness. A growing faith does not shrink back from new facts, does not persecute others, and turns doubt into sincere questioning rather than suppressing it. At its end, faith becomes not theory but experience. Paper 103 says that the certainty of such experience is unassailable and its destiny eternal (103:9.12). As a person's faith grows, it comes more and more to resemble the faith of Jesus.
ch24:50: In Closing: The Way of Loving in Order to Know
ch24:51: Faith differs from belief. Belief accepts a teaching, but faith governs the mode of living. Faith is not a certainty that man manufactures but a spiritual intuition working together with the indwelling Adjuster, and where reason halts it continues the universe journey in the company of truth. Its genuineness shows in the fruits it bears in adversity, and its example is the faith of Jesus, who trusted like a child yet was never childish. Paper 102 says that it is literally true that “Human things must be known in order to be loved, but divine things must be loved in order to be known”(102:1.1). Faith is the way of coming to know God by loving him. The next chapter examines what the kingdom of heaven is, the kingdom that is entered by this faith.

ch24:52.title: Questions for Reflection
items: 1. Among the teachings I accept as true, which actually dominate my mode of living and so have reached the level of faith (101:8.1), and which have remained at belief?
2. If Jesus asked people not to believe in him but to believe with him (196:0.13), what in the way he trusted the Father do I need to learn?
3. If honest doubt is not sin but only delay (102:1.1), how should the doubts I now hold be handled for the progress of faith?

ch25:label: Chapter 25
ch25:title: The Kingdom of Heaven
ch25:sub: The Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man
ch25:0: If salvation is a gift received by faith, and faith is the way of knowing God, where is the place of the new life into which faith leads? Jesus called it the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom of heaven is the central concept that binds together the whole of Jesus' teaching, and at the same time it is the most misunderstood. This chapter asks what The Urantia Book says the kingdom of heaven is, why it stands upon the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, and how that kingdom grows both within and around a person. The central text is Paper 170, “The Kingdom of Heaven.”
ch25:1: 1. Definition: A Kingdom Founded on Fatherhood and Brotherhood
ch25:2: In explaining Jesus' concept of the kingdom, Paper 170 first sets out its foundation. The kingdom does not begin with an institution or a territory. It begins with two truths.

ch25:3.q: The Master made it clear that the kingdom of heaven must begin with, and be centered in, the dual concept of the truth of the fatherhood of God and the correlated fact of the brotherhood of man.

ch25:4: Why these two? If God is a Father, then all men are his children; and if all are children of one Father, then men are brothers to one another. Fatherhood is the cause, and brotherhood is its result. That is why Paper 52 says that the brotherhood of man “is, after all, predicated on the recognition of the fatherhood of God”(52:6.7). Yet these two are not simply placed one after the other; on the level of personality they interlock as part and whole.

ch25:5.q: The Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man present the paradox of the part and the whole on the level of personality. God loves each individual as an individual child in the heavenly family. Yet God thus loves every individual; he is no respecter of persons, and the universality of his love brings into being a relationship of the whole, the universal brotherhood.

ch25:6: God does not love mankind as a mass but loves each person as an individual child. Yet because that love reaches all people alike, love directed to the individual becomes in itself the brotherhood that binds the whole. The kingdom of heaven is the state in which this very paradox is realized among men. The kingdom begins in the experience of the individual but never stays with the individual. In this respect the kingdom of heaven is also connected with the uniqueness of personality seen in Chapter 9. Personalities can be associated, but they are not added together. The kingdom is not a collective that melts people into a single mass but a family formed under one Father by sons and daughters who are each unique. Where the whole embraces the individual without the individual vanishing into the whole, there is the kingdom Jesus spoke of.
ch25:7: 2. Background: Ideas of the Kingdom in Jesus' Day
ch25:8: When Jesus used the expression ‘kingdom of heaven,’ it already carried many meanings. Section 1 of Paper 170 lists in turn the dual concept of the Hebrew prophets, the apocalyptic concept of the later Jews, and the teachings of the Persians, and then says that just before Jesus these ideas were combined and confused (170:1.7). Jesus did not discard the expression; he took up its highest heritage but filled it with new content. Using the word people were waiting for could open their ears, but the old expectations clinging to it constantly bred misunderstanding. The text says that even the gospel writers were colored by the belief that Jesus would soon return to establish the kingdom in power, and that his teachings were distorted for that reason (170:2.10). Jesus, however, did not connect the establishment of the kingdom with the idea of his return to this world.

ch25:9.cap: Table 25.1  Four Ideas Surrounding the Kingdom of Heaven (170:1.8–12)
rows: A present reality and a future hope to come with the Messiah, and further a supernatural world kingdom
The establishment of a divine kingdom in which good triumphs over evil at the end of the world
The confused concepts that the founders and promulgators of Christianity sought to impress upon the world

ch25:10: Of the four ideas, the third is Jesus' own. In his public teaching he used various concepts of the kingdom according to circumstances, but when teaching his apostles he always pointed in one direction.

ch25:11.q: At different times and in varying circumstances it appears that Jesus may have presented numerous concepts of the "kingdom" in his public teachings, but to his apostles he always taught the kingdom as embracing man's personal experience in relation to his fellows on earth and to the Father in heaven. Concerning the kingdom, his last word always was, "The kingdom is within you.

ch25:12: 3. Structure: The Kingdom Is Within You
ch25:13: What does it mean that the kingdom is within man? Already early in his public ministry Jesus detached the kingdom from any visible place or political order. The kingdom is wherever the spirit of God rules a person.

ch25:14.q: Be not deceived by those who come saying here is the kingdom or there is the kingdom, for my Father's kingdom concerns not things visible and material. And this kingdom is even now among you, for where the spirit of God teaches and leads the soul of man, there in reality is the kingdom of heaven.

ch25:15: When he ordained the apostles, Jesus said the same thing. The kingdom they were to proclaim was not here or there; it was “God within you”(140:1.5). The real content of the kingdom, then, is the rule of God, that is, the doing of God's will within man. The kingdom is not a territory into which man enters to live but the rule of God that enters into man and dwells there. The size of the kingdom is therefore measured not by the breadth of land but by the depth of the hearts that have yielded themselves to that rule. To make this clear, Jesus tried to change the terminology itself.

ch25:16.q: The great effort embodied in this sermon was the attempt to translate the concept of the kingdom of heaven into the ideal of the idea of doing the will of God.

ch25:17: Jesus tried to persuade his disciples to use, in place of ‘kingdom,’ its practical equivalent, ‘the will of God,’ but he did not succeed (170:2.11). He wanted to use the language of the family instead of the language of king and subjects. Jesus never once called the Father a king (169:4.1), and he said that the people of another age would better understand the gospel of the kingdom when it was presented in terms of family relationships (142:7.4).

ch25:18.q: Jesus desired to substitute for the idea of the kingdom, king, and subjects, the concept of the heavenly family, the heavenly Father, and the liberated sons of God engaged in joyful and voluntary service for their fellow men and in the sublime and intelligent worship of God the Father.

ch25:19.cap: Table 25.2  The Language of the Kingdom and the Language of the Family
rows: What Jesus sought to use instead
The heavenly family, the will of God
The heavenly Father (Jesus never called the Father a king)
Intelligent worship of God and joyful service of one's fellows
The fatherhood of God, the brotherhood of man, sonship with God

ch25:20: This change of terms is not a mere change of words. The relation of king and subject is one of power and obedience, but the relation of father and child is one of love and trust. Subjects keep the law; children delight in the father's will. When the kingdom is understood as a family, doing the will of God becomes not an imposed duty but a privilege enjoyed as a child. Here lies the reason Jesus cared so deeply about this change.
ch25:21: 4. The Entrance: Entered by Faith, Grown by Forgiveness
ch25:22: If the kingdom is an inner experience, how does a person enter it? Jesus taught that by faith the believer enters the kingdom now (170:2.20). And he pictured the character of that faith in the figure of a little child.

ch25:23.q: But I say to you in all sincerity: Unless you seek entrance into the kingdom with the faith and trusting dependence of a little child, you shall in no wise gain admission.

ch25:24.cap: Table 25.3  What Is Needed to Enter the Kingdom (170:2.20–23)
rows: To come as a little child, to receive sonship as a gift, and to submit to the Father's will in trust
Thirst for righteousness, a change of mind, the motive to be like God
God has already forgiven; in forgiving our fellows we gain the capacity to receive that forgiveness

ch25:25: The door is faith, but life within the kingdom opens through forgiveness. Section 3 of Paper 170 explains how the righteousness of the kingdom is attained as a process of receiving God's forgiveness.

ch25:26.q: Faith is the price you pay for entrance into the family of God; but forgiveness is the act of God which accepts your faith as the price of admission. And the reception of the forgiveness of God by a kingdom believer involves a definite and actual experience and consists in the following four steps, the kingdom steps of inner righteousness

ch25:27.cap: Table 25.4  The Four Kingdom Steps of Inner Righteousness (170:3.4–7)
rows: God's forgiveness is actually experienced in the measure that a person forgives his fellows (170:3.4)
One does not truly forgive his fellows unless he loves them as himself (170:3.5)
To love one's neighbor as oneself is the highest ethics (170:3.6)
Moral conduct, true righteousness, is the natural result of such love (170:3.7)

ch25:28: These four steps have the same shape as the order of salvation seen in Chapter 23. Righteousness is not the condition for entering the kingdom but the result that love bears within the kingdom. Forgiveness comes first, love next, and righteousness last of all. When a person forgives his fellows, he creates in his own soul the capacity to receive God's forgiveness (170:2.23). Within the kingdom, therefore, receiving forgiveness and giving it are not separate acts. And so Jesus summed up the relation between religion and ethics in this way.

ch25:29.q: It therefore is evident that the true and inner religion of the kingdom unfailingly and increasingly tends to manifest itself in practical avenues of social service. Jesus taught a living religion that impelled its believers to engage in the doing of loving service. But Jesus did not put ethics in the place of religion. He taught religion as a cause and ethics as a result.

ch25:30: If ethics is put in the place of the cause, religion becomes a list of moral rules, and people look for their own righteousness in keeping the rules. Jesus reversed that order. Inner communion with God is the cause, and loving service to one's neighbor is its result. Trying to manufacture the result produces hypocrisy, but when the cause is genuine, the result follows of itself.
ch25:31: 5. Unfolding: The Twofold Nature and Five Phases of the Kingdom
ch25:32: The kingdom is within man now, but that does not mean it is complete. One Sabbath afternoon Jesus explained the twofold nature of the kingdom in two phases.

ch25:33.q: First. The kingdom of God in this world, the supreme desire to do the will of God, the unselfish love of man which yields the good fruits of improved ethical and moral conduct.

ch25:34.q: Second. The kingdom of God in heaven, the goal of mortal believers, the estate wherein the love for God is perfected, and wherein the will of God is done more divinely.

ch25:35: The kingdom in this world and the kingdom in heaven are not two different realms but two phases of one kingdom. Like seed and fruit, what begins on earth is completed in heaven. Jesus compared the time between them to a growing seed.

ch25:36.q: This new kingdom is like a seed growing in the good soil of a field. It does not attain full fruit quickly. There is an interval of time between the establishment of the kingdom in the soul of man and that hour when the kingdom ripens into the full fruit of everlasting righteousness and eternal salvation.

ch25:37: In the same sermon Jesus set out the kingdom in five phases, or epochs (170:4.1). Beginning with the inner experience of the individual, it passes through the social brotherhood of believers and the brotherhood of invisible spiritual beings, and reaches a new social order and the age of light and life.

ch25:38.cap: Table 25.5  The Five Phases of the Kingdom (170:4.2–6)
rows: The believer's inner spiritual experience in fellowship with God the Father
The enlarging brotherhood of gospel believers, with enhanced morals and quickened ethics
The brotherhood of invisible spiritual beings prevailing on earth and in heaven
The dawn of a new social order in which the will of God is more perfectly fulfilled
The age of light and life, the future spiritual age on earth

ch25:39: Whenever Jesus speaks of the kingdom, we must always examine which of these five phases he has in mind (170:4.7). And the way these five phases follow one another is not revolution but transformation. The kingdom does not impose institutions from above; it changes the human will from within. That is why the progress of the kingdom seems slow. But the text tells us not to become discouraged by the apparently slow progress of the kingdom idea on Urantia (170:4.14). Evolution undergoes sudden changes in both the material and the spiritual worlds, and the bestowal of Jesus was itself such an unexpected event.

ch25:40.q: By this process of gradually changing man's will and thus affecting human decisions, Michael and his associates are likewise gradually but certainly changing the entire course of human evolution, social and otherwise.

ch25:41: 6. Consequence: The Kingdom and Its Social Fruits
ch25:42: If the kingdom begins within the individual, does it have nothing to do with society? It does not. The religion of the kingdom is personal, but its fruits are familial and social (170:3.10). There is an order, however: social results must grow of themselves out of the inner experience of the individual. Paper 170 brings out Jesus' meaning by contrasting what the kingdom was understood to be in each tradition.

ch25:43.q: The kingdom, to the Jews, was the Israelite community; to the gentiles it became the Christian church. To Jesus the kingdom was the sum of those individuals who had confessed their faith in the fatherhood of God, thereby declaring their wholehearted dedication to the doing of the will of God, thus becoming members of the spiritual brotherhood of man.

ch25:44: The church may be a natural social product of the kingdom. But “membership in the church does not necessarily mean fellowship in the kingdom; one is spiritual, the other mainly social”(170:5.18). The historical relation between the kingdom and the church, and the process by which the concept of the kingdom came to be replaced by the church, are treated in Chapter 31. Jesus himself foresaw these social fruits.

ch25:45.q: The Master fully realized that certain social results would appear in the world as a consequence of the spread of the gospel of the kingdom; but he intended that all such desirable social manifestations should appear as unconscious and inevitable outgrowths, or natural fruits, of this inner personal experience of individual believers, this purely spiritual fellowship and communion with the divine spirit which indwells and activates all such believers.

ch25:46: What matters here is that the kingdom does not coincide with the boundaries of any organization. The boundaries of the kingdom are drawn in the human heart that seeks to do the will of God.
ch25:47: In Closing: The Kingdom as a Family
ch25:48: The kingdom of heaven stands upon two truths, the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. Jesus detached that kingdom from any visible place or political order and located it where the spirit of God teaches and leads man, in the inner life of the person in whom the will of God is done. A person enters it through childlike faith, and bears the fruit of righteousness by forgiving his fellows and so experiencing God's forgiveness. The kingdom begins in this world and is completed in heaven, growing from the experience of the individual, through the brotherhood of society, toward the age of light and life. Jesus said that whoever enters that kingdom already has eternal life (146:3.7). The next chapter examines that eternal life: survival beyond death and the ascent toward Paradise.

ch25:49.title: Questions for Reflection
items: 1. If Jesus sought to use the term ‘the will of God’ in place of ‘kingdom’ (170:2.11), what concretely does it mean for the kingdom of heaven to be realized within me today?
2. If God's forgiveness is experienced in the measure that I forgive my fellows (170:3.4), what meaning does a person I have not yet forgiven hold for my spiritual growth?
3. If membership in the church is not the same as fellowship in the kingdom (170:5.18), how do I recognize the brotherhood of believers?

ch26:label: Chapter 26
ch26:title: Eternal Life
ch26:0: The doctrines of salvation, faith, and the kingdom of heaven all look toward one point. Does man survive death, and if he survives, where does he go? The Urantia Book answers this question in more detail than any other revelation. It tells where each element of a person goes at the moment of death, how one awakens on the mansion worlds, and what stages one passes through on the way to Paradise. Yet what this chapter asks first is not the details of that route but its logic. What is eternal life, why is it given, and what determines it?
ch26:2: Eternal life is commonly thought of as a life that begins after death. Jesus put it differently. Eternal life becomes a person's possession the moment he enters the kingdom.

ch26:3.q: The way from the earth life to the eternal estate has not been made plain to you, but there is a way, there always has been, and I have come to make that way new and living. He who enters the kingdom has eternal life already—he shall never perish.

ch26:4: The key word is ‘already.’ Before it is a future reward, eternal life is a present gift. After his resurrection Jesus stressed the same point. It is not enough merely to rejoice in the fact that he has risen.

ch26:5.q: You rejoice to know that I am the resurrection and the life, but this will avail you nothing unless you are first born of the eternal spirit, thereby coming to possess, by faith, the gift of eternal life. If you are the faith sons of my Father, you shall never die; you shall not perish.

ch26:6: Eternal life is therefore linked in a single chain with salvation in Chapter 23, faith in Chapter 24, and the kingdom in Chapter 25. To be born of the spirit by faith is salvation; the place so entered is the kingdom; and the life already possessed within it is eternal life. This assurance changes a person's earthly life. Jesus told Thomas that those who know God and believe the gospel “have already received the assurances of eternal life”(176:3.2). Though nations fall and an age ends, that life is not shaken. This does not erase the future, however. The life that begins now is the first chapter of the life still to unfold. On the day he foretold the destruction of Jerusalem, Jesus spoke of the two together.

ch26:7.q: I have brought the kingdom of heaven to you here on earth, but I declare that all of you who by faith enter therein and remain therein by the living service of truth, shall surely ascend to the worlds on high and sit with me in the spirit kingdom of our Father.

ch26:8: Present possession and future ascent are not two different promises but two aspects of one life. Entering by faith is its beginning, remaining by the living service of truth is the way that life is kept, and ascending to the worlds on high is its completion.

ch26:9.cap: Table 26.1  The Present and the Future of Eternal Life
rows: He who enters the kingdom has eternal life already
Being born of the eternal spirit and possessing the gift by faith
Those who are God-knowing and gospel-believing have already received the assurances
It becomes easier every day to do the right thing
Ascending to the worlds on high and reaching the spirit kingdom of the Father

ch26:11: If eternal life is a gift, what in man receives that gift and passes beyond death? The body returns to dust. The material mind also ceases to function along with the brain. Jesus placed the ground of survival in the Father's spirit within man.

ch26:12.q: You survive your life in the material world of the flesh because you are identified with the Father's living spirit, the gift of eternal life.

ch26:13: Survival happens not because of some immortality man possesses by nature, but because man identifies himself with the indwelling spirit. What that identification produces is the soul. The origin of the soul was treated in Chapter 12. Through the choices he makes day by day on earth, a person grows this soul, and the soul becomes the vessel of survival. Survival, therefore, is not decided suddenly at the moment of death; it is prepared by a lifetime. What is important here is the fact that at the moment of death the factors of survival are divided and held in two keepings. Describing the resurrection halls of the first mansion world, Paper 47 says this.

ch26:14.q: The creature mind-matrix and the passive potentials of identity are present in the morontia soul intrusted to the keeping of the seraphic destiny guardians. And it is the reuniting of the morontia-soul trust of the seraphim and the spirit-mind trust of the Adjuster that reassembles creature personality and constitutes resurrection of a sleeping survivor.

ch26:15.cap: Table 26.2  Where Each Element of a Person Goes After Death
rows: Returns to the elemental world of its origin; no part of the reassembly
Goes to Divinington bearing the memory transcription of the mortal career
Remains in the custody of the destiny guardian
Reassembled when Adjuster and soul are reunited

ch26:16: What deserves notice in this table is that survival is not the solitary act of a single being. The Adjuster keeps the spirit-mind, the seraphim keep the soul, and in the resurrection halls many universe personalities join the two again. Human survival is a work accomplished together by God, the celestial beings, and man himself. At the same time, memories without spiritual meaning disappear and only experiences of value remain. Death is not an event that robs a person of something, but an event that separates what will endure forever from what will pass away.
ch26:18: Death is not an end but a sleep. Survivors are unconscious between death and repersonalization, and on awakening they are unaware of the time that has passed. Those who have personal guardians awaken on the mansion worlds on the third period, while those who do not awaken together at the end of a dispensation (30:4.11).

ch26:19.q: The passing of time is of no moment to sleeping mortals; they are wholly unconscious and oblivious to the length of their rest. On reassembly of personality at the end of an age, those who have slept five thousand years will react no differently than those who have rested five days.

ch26:20: And the one who awakens is not someone else. The very life that stopped at death continues as it was.

ch26:21.q: On the mansion worlds the resurrected mortal survivors resume their lives just where they left off when overtaken by death. When you go from Urantia to the first mansion world, you will notice considerable change, but if you had come from a more normal and progressive sphere of time, you would hardly notice the difference except for the fact that you were in possession of a different body

ch26:22: The phrase ‘just where they left off’ means two things together: that death does not suddenly make a person complete, and that none of the growth achieved on earth is wasted. The mansion worlds are a school that supplies what could not be fully learned on earth, and the ascent is not a new start cut off from earthly life but its continuation. A detailed account of the mansion worlds is found in Paper 47; here only the principle is noted. What begins on this world continues on those worlds. The Urantia Book also distinguishes three kinds of death in relation to human survival.

ch26:23.cap: Table 26.3  Three Kinds of Death Related to Personality Survival (112:3.1–4)
rows: When a mortal has finally rejected survival (112:3.2)
The Adjuster is liberated; from the cosmic standpoint the person is already dead
When the circuits of the will mind are irretrievably broken (112:3.3)
The Adjuster departs, but the soul may survive according to previous choices
When the mind ceases to function as an intellectual mechanism (112:3.4)
The Adjuster goes to Divinington and the soul is entrusted to the guardian

ch26:24: 4. The Condition: Survival Is a Choice
ch26:25: The first kind of death in Table 26.3 shows that survival is not automatic. God gives eternal life as a gift, but he does not force that gift on anyone. Paper 112 clearly distinguishes the path of survival from the one who walks it.

ch26:26.q: The energy system must continue, it has no choice; but man has everything to do with determining his own destiny. The Adjuster is truly the path to Paradise, but man himself must pursue that path by his own deciding, his freewill choosing.

ch26:27: Nor does the choice end with death. Paper 111 says that “Even after survival the ascending mortal still retains this prerogative of choosing to reject eternal life”(111:3.1), and it says that this choice remains open until fusion with the Adjuster.
ch26:28: If the choice weighs so much, must a person live in fear? The Urantia Book stresses that the choice is handled fairly and mercifully. To those who through no fault of their own, because of the accidents of time and material handicaps, could not grow sufficiently on earth, an extension of probation is granted (112:5.6). When there is doubt about the advisability of advancing a person, the universe government always decides in the interest of that individual (112:5.7). And every person is assured of a true opportunity to choose.

ch26:29.q: This does not mean that human beings are to enjoy a second opportunity in the face of the rejection of a first, not at all. But it does signify that all will creatures are to experience one true opportunity to make one undoubted, self-conscious, and final choice.

ch26:30: The revealer expresses this spirit of mercy in one sentence: “We had rather assume the risk of a system rebellion than to court the hazard of depriving one struggling mortal from any evolutionary world of the eternal joy of pursuing the ascending career”(112:5.8). Yet for one who refuses survival to the end there is no resurrection. Paper 2 says that such a personality “is deprived of a continuing life vehicle”(2:3.4). Survival is both the gift of God and the choice of man. These two statements do not collide. A gift is a gift only when it is not forced, and love is love only when it is freely received. God leaves man the freedom to refuse so that this life may truly become the person's own. And that freedom finally reaches eternal confirmation in fusion with the Adjuster.

ch26:31.cap: Table 26.4  Choice and Mercy in Survival
rows: Until fusion with the Adjuster one may forsake the Father's will
Additional time is given to those who did not grow through no fault of their own
The decision is always made in the interest of the individual
Not a second chance, but a genuine opportunity for final choice
The life vehicle is lost; there is no resurrection
It signalizes the choice to do the Father's will eternally and unreservedly

ch26:33: The survivor who awakens on the mansion worlds does not remain there. Paper 30 surveys the ascending career of Adjuster-indwelt mortals in seven stages (30:4.1). The path begins on the morontia worlds of the local universe and passes through the superuniverse and Havona to Paradise.

ch26:34.cap: Table 26.5  The Seven Stages of the Ascending Career (30:4.2–8)
rows: Evolutionary beings of animal origin with ascension potential (30:4.10)
Surviving souls without guardians rest until the end of a dispensation (30:4.11)
All surviving mortals who reawaken on the mansion worlds (30:4.14)
Ascend through the spheres of the system, constellation, and universe (30:4.18)
Young spirits who are wards of the Ancients of Days (30:4.22)
Have found God and are mustered into the Mortal Corps of the Finality (30:4.31)

ch26:35: Along this path the human form changes many times. Yet the text says that even in passing from morontia to spirit, “The mind, personality, and character are unchanged by such an advance; only does the form undergo modification”(30:4.20). The same personality goes forward clothed in ever more spiritual vehicles. Each stage of the ascent therefore does not discard the previous one but builds upon it.

ch26:36.q: On earth you were a creature of flesh and blood; through the local universe you were a morontia being; through the superuniverse you were an evolving spirit; with your arrival on the receiving worlds of Havona your spiritual education begins in reality and in earnest; your eventual appearance on Paradise will be as a perfected spirit.

ch26:37: The goal of this ascent is not a place but God, who is a person. Paper 5 says that however long the path may be, man is always moving inward, and that some day, in the divine and central presence, he shall “see him, figuratively speaking, face to face”(5:1.9). Eternal life is not only living without end but drawing ever nearer to God without end. At every stage there are classes and teachers, and those who have gone ahead help those who follow. The ascent is a pilgrimage walked alone and at the same time a road walked with one's brothers. The flight to Havona alone is always made solitary (30:4.27), but the long road before and after it continues amid the morontia family and spirit companions. The brotherhood of the kingdom of heaven does not cease after death.
ch26:39: The ascender who reaches Paradise enters the Mortal Corps of the Finality. But that too is not the end. Even the revelators of Uversa confess that they do not know the ultimate destiny of the finaliters.

ch26:40.q: We of Uversa do not know the "finality destiny" of the ascendant mortals of time. At present they reside on Paradise and temporarily serve in the Corps of Light and Life, but such a tremendous course of ascendant training and such lengthy universe discipline must be designed to qualify them for even greater tests of trust and more sublime services of responsibility.

ch26:41: Paper 112 speculates cautiously about that future. The finaliters are the experiential children of the Supreme (112:7.16), and the revelators believe they will take up administrative functions in the universes of outer space now being organized (112:7.17). That the revelators say they do not know shows the honesty of this doctrine. The Urantia Book does not sketch the end of eternal life in full. It affirms only that the path is open and that its purpose lies within the infinite plan of God. Eternal life opens endlessly not into rest but into service. And all of that future is linked to the choices made on this earth today. Paper 32 closes that call in these words.

ch26:42.q: There is in the mind of God a plan which embraces every creature of all his vast domains, and this plan is an eternal purpose of boundless opportunity, unlimited progress, and endless life.

ch26:43.q: The goal of eternity is ahead! The adventure of divinity attainment lies before you! The race for perfection is on! whosoever will may enter, and certain victory will crown the efforts of every human being who will run the race of faith and trust, depending every step of the way on the leading of the indwelling Adjuster and on the guidance of that good spirit of the Universe Son, which so freely has been poured out upon all flesh.

ch26:44.cap: Table 26.6  The Logical Chain of Eternal Life
rows: Eternal life is a gift possessed now by faith
One survives by being identified with the Father's living spirit
Soul and Adjuster are reunited and the personality is reassembled
Until fusion, survival is left to the choice of man
Paradise is reached through seven stages
As finaliters, ascenders enter more sublime service

ch26:45: In Closing: A Life That Begins Now and Never Ends
ch26:46: Eternal life is not a reward first given after death. One who has been born of the spirit by faith and has entered the kingdom possesses it already. Man survives death because he identifies himself with the Father's living spirit; at the moment of death the soul and the Adjuster are held in separate keepings, and on the mansion worlds they are reunited and the same personality awakens. That survival remains to the end a matter of man's choice, but the universe government always handles that choice with mercy. The one who awakens reaches Paradise through seven stages and, as a finaliter, goes on into service not yet revealed. Thus the first four chapters of Part 6 form a single chain: salvation, faith, the kingdom, and eternal life. The next chapter examines the nature of religion, which holds this chain together within human experience.

ch26:47.title: Questions for Reflection
items: 1. If whoever enters the kingdom already has eternal life (146:3.7), how does that assurance help me see anew the things I fear today?
2. If on the mansion worlds we resume our lives just where we left off when overtaken by death (47:3.1), what growth am I now putting off?
3. If survival is both the gift of God and the choice of man (111:3.1), in what ways am I choosing eternal life in my daily decisions?

ch27:label: Chapter 27
ch27:title: The Nature of Religion
ch27:0: The earlier chapters of Part Six dealt with salvation, faith, the kingdom of heaven, and eternal life. Each of these doctrines speaks of a person's relationship with God. Where, then, does that relationship actually take place in a human life? The Urantia Book calls that place religion. Yet the religion it speaks of is not a system of churches, doctrines, or rituals. This chapter asks how The Urantia Book defines religion, from what more fundamental fact that definition arises, and what it demands of a person's life. The three chapters that follow, on worship, prayer, and healing, all rest on the definition laid down here.
ch27:1: 1. What Religion Is Not, and What It Is
ch27:2: When Paper 101, “The Real Nature of Religion”, sets out to define religion, it first clears away what religion is not. Religion is not a system of philosophy proved by reason, nor is it an ecstasy enjoyed only by a few mystics. With these two misconceptions removed, the revelator sets down a brief definition.

ch27:3.q: Religion is the experiencing of divinity in the consciousness of a moral being of evolutionary origin; it represents true experience with eternal realities in time, the realization of spiritual satisfactions while yet in the flesh.

ch27:4: The key word in this definition is experience. Religion is not knowing about something; it is undergoing divinity directly in consciousness. That is why The Urantia Book sharply distinguishes religion from agreement with doctrine. True religion is “not a mere intellectual assent to any body of dogmatic doctrines” (101:2.13). Nor does religion remain a passive feeling of dependence on God.

ch27:5.q: But religion is not merely a passive feeling of "absolute dependence" and "surety of survival"; it is a living and dynamic experience of divinity attainment predicated on humanity service.

ch27:6: To call religion dynamic is to say that it turns a person outward rather than shutting him up within himself. Paper 5 distinguishes religious from nonreligious activity by the direction in which the self is turned.

ch27:7.q: All nonreligious human activities seek to bend the universe to the distorting service of self; the truly religious individual seeks to identify the self with the universe and then to dedicate the activities of this unified self to the service of the universe family of fellow beings, human and superhuman.

ch27:8: Because experience is alive, it reaches across the whole of life. Paper 100 settles this point in a single sentence: “Religion is not a specific function of life; rather is it a mode of living” (100:6.1). Religion is not a compartment one enters once a week; it is the very direction of a life devoted to the reality a person holds to be of supreme value.

ch27:9.cap: Table 27.1  Four Misconceptions about Religion and the Text's Answer
rows: Religion is a system of philosophic belief proved by reason
Religion is not the product of reason, but viewed from within, it is altogether reasonable
Religion is an ecstatic experience enjoyed only by mystics
Religion is born neither of mystic meditations nor of isolated contemplations
Religion is intellectual assent to doctrine
Religion consists not in theologic propositions but in spiritual insight and the soul's trust
Religion is a passive feeling of dependence
It is a dynamic experience of divinity attainment predicated on humanity service

ch27:10: 2. The Root of Religion: The Indwelling Spirit and Moral Choice
ch27:11: Where, then, does such experience come from? The Urantia Book answers: from God within man, the Thought Adjuster. The seed of religion is not something a person has cultivated on his own; it sprouts because God has first come to dwell in the mind that hungers for him.

ch27:12.q: The germs of true religion originate in the domain of man's moral consciousness, and they are revealed in the growth of man's spiritual insight, that faculty of human personality which accrues as a consequence of the presence of the God-revealing Thought Adjuster in the God-hungry mortal mind.

ch27:13: Yet the Adjuster has no separate organ for religious experience. The Urantia Book states that “there is no mystic religious faculty for the reception or expression of religious emotions” (101:1.2). The Adjuster works through man's ordinary mind, and through thought rather than through emotion.

ch27:14.q: The divine spirit makes contact with mortal man, not by feelings or emotions, but in the realm of the highest and most spiritualized thinking. It is your thoughts, not your feelings, that lead you Godward.

ch27:15: This fact corrects the common notion that religion is the same as heightened emotion. Warm feelings may accompany religious experience, but they are not its essence. Religion takes place in the highest thinking of the mind, and that thinking finally shows itself in choice. Paper 103, “The Reality of Religious Experience”, locates the moment when religious experience first appears in the conflict between selfishness and unselfishness.

ch27:16.q: When a moral being chooses to be unselfish when confronted by the urge to be selfish, that is primitive religious experience. No animal can make such a choice

ch27:17: Here the order of religion comes to light. Religion does not first build a system of belief and then go looking for values. “Religion is primarily a pursuit of values, and then there formulates a system of interpretative beliefs” (103:1.4). That is why people who divide endlessly over creeds can readily unite on values and goals: the root of religion lies not in creed but in the choice of values that the indwelling spirit awakens.
ch27:18: For the same reason religion is personal and yet draws people together. Because a fragment of God of identical nature indwells every person, unity of experience is possible; because every personality is unique, interpretations are bound to differ. “A group of mortals can experience spiritual unity, but they can never attain philosophic uniformity” (103:1.1). This principle anticipates the contrast, taken up below, between the religion of the spirit and the religion of authority.

ch27:19.cap: Table 27.2  The Order in Which Religious Experience Arises
rows: The God-revealing Thought Adjuster is present in the God-hungry mind
Contact is made not by feelings but in the realm of the highest thinking
Choosing to be unselfish when confronted by the urge to be selfish: primitive religious experience
Religion begins as a pursuit of values
Then a system of interpretative beliefs, that is, theology, is formulated

ch27:20: 3. Three Forms of Religion: Fear, Authority, and Spirit
ch27:21: If religion is experience, the quality of that experience differs from person to person and from people to people. On the way past Caesarea-Philippi toward Phoenicia, Jesus taught this difference systematically. Section 5 of Paper 155, “The Discourse on True Religion”, first observes that the religions of the world have a double origin, natural and revelatory, and then sets out three forms in which the religious urge appears. The third of these is true religion.

ch27:22.q: 3. True religion—the religion of revelation. The revelation of supernatural values, a partial insight into eternal realities, a glimpse of the goodness and beauty of the infinite character of the Father in heaven—the religion of the spirit as demonstrated in human experience.

ch27:23.cap: Table 27.3  Three Forms of the Religious Urge (155:5.2–5.6)
rows: The seminatural, instinctive urge to fear mysterious energies; the religion of fear
Advancing religious concepts and practices; the religion of the mind
The religion of revelation; a partial insight into eternal realities
Difference between the second and third
The religion of the mind is upheld by ecclesiastical authority
The religion of the spirit is wholly based on experience

ch27:24: Paper 5 states the same distinction in the language of motive. Evolutionary religion drives men forward in the God quest by the power of fear, while revealed religion draws those who crave to become like God toward a God of love (5:4.1). The two differ in method but are alike in motive, and revelation comes along the road that evolution has prepared. This is also why Paper 103 says that four kinds of religion exist side by side on Urantia today: natural religion, revealed religion, a practical religion that mixes the two, and a philosophic religion built by reason (103:0.3–0.7).
ch27:25: 4. The Religion of Authority and the Religion of the Spirit
ch27:26: What Jesus stressed most in this discourse was the contrast between the religion of the mind and the religion of the spirit. The religion of the mind is easy, because it leans on established authority and asks only for intellectual assent. The religion of the spirit asks for the whole person.

ch27:27.q: The religion of the spirit means effort, struggle, conflict, faith, determination, love, loyalty, and progress. The religion of the mind—the theology of authority—requires little or none of these exertions from its formal believers.

ch27:28: The two religions also face time in opposite directions. The religion of authority finds its security in guarding statements already fixed in the past; the religion of the spirit stays open to truth not yet arrived. Jesus put the difference this way.

ch27:29.q: The religion of the mind ties you hopelessly to the past; the religion of the spirit consists in progressive revelation and ever beckons you on toward higher and holier achievements in spiritual ideals and eternal realities.

ch27:30: This does not mean that Jesus despised those who remain in the religion of authority. He said that the Father “will ever respond to the faintest flicker of faith” (155:6.17). The Father honors even the superstitious emotions of primitive man and the feeble attempts of honest souls who, out of fear, do not get beyond intellectual assent. But those who have been called out of darkness into the light are expected to have a faith that governs body, mind, and spirit together.
ch27:31: This contrast does not end with the individual; it carries over into the question of human unity. The religion of authority divides people because it demands uniformity of belief. The religion of the spirit draws together people of differing beliefs because it requires only unity of experience.

ch27:32.q: The religions of authority require of men uniformity in belief, but this is impossible of realization in the present state of the world. The religion of the spirit requires only unity of experience—uniformity of destiny—making full allowance for diversity of belief.

ch27:33.cap: Table 27.4  The Religion of Authority and the Religion of the Spirit
rows: Religion of authority (religion of the mind)
A passive and purely intellectual assent
Effort, struggle, faith, determination, love, loyalty, and progress
Through progressive revelation, beckons you on toward higher achievements
A present feeling of security, at the price of spiritual freedom
Leaves you forever free to follow the truth
Draws men together and makes them understandingly sympathetic
Unity of experience, that is, uniformity of destiny

ch27:34: 5. Religion and Theology, Philosophy, and Science
ch27:35: If religion is experience, what is theology? The Urantia Book does not discard theology, but it fixes its place clearly. Theology is an honest attempt to interpret experience, and it cannot take the place of experience. Hence, “No matter how illusory and erroneous one's theology, one's religion may be wholly genuine and everlastingly true” (103:9.2). Conversely, when theology takes the place of experience, religion loses its life.

ch27:36.q: Notwithstanding the mythologic vagaries and the psychologic illusions of the intellectual content of religion, the metaphysical assumptions of error and the techniques of self-deception, the political distortions and the socioeconomic perversions of the philosophic content of religion, the spiritual experience of personal religion remains genuine and valid.

ch27:37: This sentence candidly admits the many errors that have piled up in the history of religion, yet it safeguards religion itself. That religionists have believed much that was false does not invalidate religion, because religion rests not on interpretation but on the recognition and experience of values (103:1.5). For the same reason, religion cannot be judged from outside. The revelator says that religion “can never be observed, much less understood, from the outside” (101:2.16). Among those who have had a similar experience no argument about God is needed, and to one who lacks such assurance no argument is convincing.

ch27:38.q: When theology masters religion, religion dies; it becomes a doctrine instead of a life. The mission of theology is merely to facilitate the self-consciousness of personal spiritual experience.

ch27:39: Nor is religion at war with science or philosophy. The three are different ways of approaching reality, and revelation binds them together.

ch27:40.q: Reason is the proof of science, faith the proof of religion, logic the proof of philosophy, but revelation is validated only by human experience. Science yields knowledge; religion yields happiness; philosophy yields unity

ch27:41.cap: Table 27.5  Three Paths to Reality, and Revelation
rows: Compensates for the absence of the morontia viewpoint (101:2.2)
Confirms the experiential harmony of the three approaches (101:2.8)
Affirms that the First Cause of science and the God of salvation are one and the same Deity (101:2.7)

ch27:43: Experience cannot be observed from outside. How, then, can true religion be recognized? Paper 101 says that genuine faith shows itself in the way a person reacts, and it lists twelve marks. Every one of them takes the form of 'in spite of.' Religion does not remove adversity; in the midst of adversity it produces a response that rises above the natural animal reaction.

ch27:44.cap: Table 27.6  Some of the Twelve Marks of Genuine Faith (101:3.4–3.16)
rows: Causes ethics and morals to progress
Produces a sublime trust in the goodness of God
Baffling diseases and acute physical suffering
Exhibits inexplicable poise and sustaining tranquillity
Contributes to the continued survival of altruism
In spite of anything and everything

ch27:45: At the head of the twelve marks the revelator explains what they reveal: the fact that a person's soul is growing.

ch27:46.q: Through religious faith the soul of man reveals itself and demonstrates the potential divinity of its emerging nature by the characteristic manner in which it induces the mortal personality to react to certain trying intellectual and testing social situations.

ch27:47: The state to which all twelve marks point is an unshakable peace. This peace is not the calm that comes from having no problems; it is the stability that comes from being rooted in the goodness of the universe even in the midst of problems.

ch27:48.q: One of the most amazing earmarks of religious living is that dynamic and sublime peace, that peace which passes all human understanding, that cosmic poise which betokens the absence of all doubt and turmoil. Such levels of spiritual stability are immune to disappointment.

ch27:49: This fruit does not cut a person off from the world. The religionist's detachment from trivial things does not lead to social isolation or to the loss of a sense of humor. Paper 100 says the very opposite.

ch27:50.q: Genuine religion takes nothing away from human existence, but it does add new meanings to all of life; it generates new types of enthusiasm, zeal, and courage.

ch27:51: Jesus, too, told his hearers not to try to prove by argument that they know God. Such evidence cannot be produced deliberately. Jesus named only two proofs. One is “The fruits of the spirit of God showing forth in your daily routine life” (155:6.15); the other is the fact that one's entire life plan has been risked without reserve on the adventure of survival after death (155:6.16). The proof of religion lies not in words but in fruits and devotion. And Jesus described the experience that bears such fruit in these words.

ch27:52.q: the supernal experience of finding God for yourself, in yourself, and of yourself, and of doing all this as a fact in your own personal experience.

ch27:53: In Closing: Experience, the Way to Know God
ch27:54: The Urantia Book's teaching on religion forms a single chain. Religion is the experiencing of divinity in consciousness. That experience springs from the Adjuster who indwells a person, and it first appears as a moral choice that rises above selfishness. According to the quality of the experience, religion divides into the religion of fear, the religion of authority, and the religion of the spirit, and Jesus called people to the religion of the spirit, which asks for the whole person. Theology, philosophy, and science interpret and assist this experience but cannot replace it, and true religion proves itself by its fruits in adversity. The act in which this experience turns most purely toward God is worship. The next chapter examines worship, which The Urantia Book calls 'the highest privilege and the first duty of all created intelligences.'

ch27:55.title: Questions for Reflection
items: 1. In light of the words “Religion is not a specific function of life; rather is it a mode of living” (100:6.1), is religion in my life closer to a function or to a mode of living?
2. Between the security offered by the religion of authority and the freedom offered by the religion of the spirit (155:6.5), which do I choose more readily, and why?
3. If the moment of choosing to be unselfish in the face of the urge to be selfish is the primitive form of religious experience (103:2.8), which of the choices before me today is such a moment?
